Climate and Genetic Variation - Raster Data Homework

Author

Dez Waag

Published

November 12, 2026

Abstract

This analysis used WorldClim temperature and precipitation rasters to examine relationships between climate and genetic variation in the beetle Araptus attenuatus and the plant Euphorbia lomelii in Baja California and Sonora. Beetle genetic variation decreased with increasing temperature, the only significant association in the unadjusted correlation tests; no significant associations were found for the plant.

Introduction

Climate may help explain differences in genetic variation among populations by influencing the conditions organisms experience across their range. This analysis focuses on the beetle Araptus attenuatus and the plant Euphorbia lomelii at sampling sites in Baja California and Sonora. By combining site data with climate rasters, I examine whether warmer or wetter locations are associated with higher or lower genetic variation and whether similar patterns appear in both species.

The table below outlines the climate variables and genetic variation measures used in the four correlation tests.

Climate variable Genetic variation variable
Annual mean temperature Beetle: GenVarArapat
Annual precipitation Beetle: GenVarArapat
Annual mean temperature Plant: GenVarEuphli
Annual precipitation Plant: GenVarEuphli

Methods

Data

Sampling data from the course repository included genetic variation for the beetle Araptus attenuatus (GenVarArapat) and the plant Euphorbia lomelii (GenVarEuphli) at sites in Baja California and Sonora. Site coordinates were converted into spatial points using WGS 84. WorldClim bioclimatic data were downloaded using the geodata package (Fick and Hijmans, 2017). Annual mean temperature (°C) and annual precipitation (mm) were selected and cropped to the study region using the boundaries specified below.

library(terra)
library(tidyterra)
library(sf)
library(tidyverse)
library(geodata)

beetle_url <- "https://dyerlabteaching.github.io/CourseData/Spatial/AraptusDispersalBias.csv"

beetles <- read_csv(beetle_url) |>
  st_as_sf(
    coords = c("Longitude", "Latitude"),
    crs = 4326 )

Analysis

Temperature and precipitation were mapped separately, with the sampling sites overlaid on each map. Climate values were extracted from the raster cell containing each site and added to the sampling dataset. Pearson correlations were used to test the relationship of each climate variable with genetic variation in each species. Tests were two-sided, and p-values were evaluated without adjustment for multiple testing. A scatterplot with a fitted linear regression and confidence band was used to display the significant beetle–temperature relationship.

site_climate <- terra::extract(
  climate_crop,
  terra::vect(beetles),
  ID = FALSE )

beetles <- beetles |>
  mutate(
    Temperature = site_climate$Temperature,
    Precipitation = site_climate$Precipitation )

beetles |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  select(Site, Temperature, Precipitation, GenVarArapat, GenVarEuphli) |>
  print(n = Inf)

Results

The correlation results summarize the direction and strength of the relationships between climate and genetic variation in each species (Table 1). The significant negative association between temperature and beetle genetic variation is shown in Figure 3.

correlation_results <- tibble(
  Species = c("Beetle", "Beetle", "Plant", "Plant"),
  Climate = c(
    "Temperature", "Precipitation",
    "Temperature", "Precipitation" ),
  r = c(
    unname(beetle_temp$estimate),
    unname(beetle_precip$estimate),
    unname(plant_temp$estimate),
    unname(plant_precip$estimate) ),
  t = c(
    unname(beetle_temp$statistic),
    unname(beetle_precip$statistic),
    unname(plant_temp$statistic),
    unname(plant_precip$statistic) ),
  df = c(
    unname(beetle_temp$parameter),
    unname(beetle_precip$parameter),
    unname(plant_temp$parameter),
    unname(plant_precip$parameter) ),
  p = c(
    beetle_temp$p.value,
    beetle_precip$p.value,
    plant_temp$p.value,
    plant_precip$p.value ) )

knitr::kable(
  correlation_results,
  digits = c(0, 0, 3, 3, 0, 4),
  col.names = c(
    "Species", "Climate variable", "Pearson's r",
    "t", "df", "p-value" ) )
ggplot(
  data = st_drop_geometry(beetles),
  aes(x = Temperature, y = GenVarArapat) ) +
  geom_point(
    color = "#B10026",
    size = 3,
    alpha = 0.8 ) +
  geom_smooth(
    method = "lm",
    formula = y ~ x,
    se = TRUE,
    color = "black",
    fill = "grey75" ) +
  labs(
    title = "Beetle Genetic Variation and Temperature",
    x = "Annual mean temperature (°C)",
    y = "Beetle genetic variation" ) +
  theme_minimal()
N <- nrow(beetles)

temp_min <- format(min(beetles$Temperature), digits = 3)
temp_max <- format(max(beetles$Temperature), digits = 3)

precip_min <- format(min(beetles$Precipitation), digits = 3)
precip_max <- format(max(beetles$Precipitation), digits = 3)

bt_r <- format(unname(beetle_temp$estimate), digits = 3)
bt_t <- format(unname(beetle_temp$statistic), digits = 3)
bt_p <- format(beetle_temp$p.value, digits = 3)

bp_r <- format(unname(beetle_precip$estimate), digits = 3)
bp_p <- format(beetle_precip$p.value, digits = 3)

pt_r <- format(unname(plant_temp$estimate), digits = 3)
pt_p <- format(plant_temp$p.value, digits = 3)

pp_r <- format(unname(plant_precip$estimate), digits = 3)
pp_p <- format(plant_precip$p.value, digits = 3)

The 31 sampling sites ranged from 18.6 to 24.4 °C in annual mean temperature and from 87 to 405 mm in annual precipitation. The climate maps show the regional patterns and sampling locations (Figure 1; Figure 2). Beetle genetic variation was negatively associated with temperature (Pearson’s r = -0.412, t = -2.43, p = 0.0214), with lower genetic variation generally occurring at warmer sites (Figure 3). Its relationship with precipitation was also negative but was not statistically significant (r = -0.327, p = 0.0725). Plant genetic variation was not significantly associated with temperature (r = 0.15, p = 0.42) or precipitation (r = 0.0111, p = 0.953). Of the four tests, only the beetle–temperature relationship was significant at the unadjusted 0.05 level (Table 1).

Interpretation

The clearest pattern was that beetle genetic variation tended to be lower at warmer sites. Plant genetic variation did not show a significant relationship with either temperature or precipitation, and precipitation was not significantly associated with beetle genetic variation. The species therefore did not show the same observed pattern, although these separate tests do not establish that their responses to climate are statistically different. Temperature may be relevant to the beetle’s genetic variation, but this correlation does not show that warmer conditions directly cause lower variation. Other factors, such as population size, isolation, and movement between populations, could also contribute to the pattern. Because the tests were not adjusted for multiple comparisons, the significant result should be interpreted cautiously.

Questions

TipQuestion 1: Color palettes

Which kind of palette (sequential, diverging, or qualitative) did you use for each map, and why does it fit that variable?

Both maps use sequential palettes because temperature and precipitation are continuous variables that progress from lower to higher values. The temperature map moves from light yellow to dark red as temperatures increase, while the precipitation map moves from light blue to dark blue as precipitation increases.

TipQuestion 2: Interpreting raster cells

Each climate value you extracted comes from a single cell about 1 km on a side. What does that one number actually represent for the beetles or plants at that site, and when could that be misleading?

Each extracted value represents an estimate of long-term annual mean temperature or annual precipitation for the raster cell containing the sampling site, rather than a direct measurement of conditions experienced by individual beetles or plants. This can be misleading when local conditions vary within the cell, such as shaded versus exposed areas or differences in elevation, or when seasonal extremes are hidden by the annual summary.

References

Fick, S.E. and R.J. Hijmans. 2017. WorldClim 2: new 1km spatial resolution climate surfaces for global land areas. International Journal of Climatology 37(12): 4302–4315.

Climate may help explain differences in genetic variation among populations by influencing the conditions organisms experience across their range. This analysis focuses on the beetle *Araptus attenuatus* and the plant *Euphorbia lomelii* at sampling sites in Baja California and Sonora. By combining site data with climate rasters, I examine whether warmer or wetter locations are associated with higher or lower genetic variation and whether similar patterns appear in both species.

## Methods

### Data

Sampling data from the course repository included genetic variation for the beetle *Araptus attenuatus* (`GenVarArapat`) and the plant *Euphorbia lomelii* (`GenVarEuphli`) at sites in Baja California and Sonora. Site coordinates were converted into spatial points using WGS 84. WorldClim bioclimatic data were downloaded using the `geodata` package (Fick and Hijmans, 2017). Annual mean temperature (°C) and annual precipitation (mm) were selected and cropped to the study region using the boundaries specified below.

```{r}
#| label: load-sampling-sites
#| message: false

library(terra)
library(tidyterra)
library(sf)
library(tidyverse)
library(geodata)

beetle_url <- "https://dyerlabteaching.github.io/CourseData/Spatial/AraptusDispersalBias.csv"

beetles <- read_csv(beetle_url) |>
  st_as_sf(
    coords = c("Longitude", "Latitude"),
    crs = 4326 )

beetles
```

```{r}
#| label: load-climate-data

dir.create("data", showWarnings = FALSE)

climate <- geodata::worldclim_tile(
  var = "bio",
  lon = -112,
  lat = 26,
  path = "data" )

climate
```


```{r}
#| label: crop-climate-data

climate_selected <- climate[[c(1, 12)]]

names(climate_selected) <- c("Temperature", "Precipitation")

study_extent <- terra::ext(-116, -109, 22, 30)

climate_crop <- terra::crop(climate_selected, study_extent)

climate_crop
```

### Analysis

Temperature and precipitation were mapped separately, with the sampling sites overlaid on each map. Climate values were extracted from the raster cell containing each site and added to the sampling dataset. Pearson correlations were used to test the relationship of each climate variable with genetic variation in each species. Tests were two-sided, and p-values were evaluated without adjustment for multiple testing. A scatterplot with a fitted linear regression and confidence band was used to display the significant beetle–temperature relationship.

```{r}
#| label: extract-site-climate

site_climate <- terra::extract(
  climate_crop,
  terra::vect(beetles),
  ID = FALSE )

beetles <- beetles |>
  mutate(
    Temperature = site_climate$Temperature,
    Precipitation = site_climate$Precipitation )

beetles |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  select(Site, Temperature, Precipitation, GenVarArapat, GenVarEuphli) |>
  print(n = Inf)
```

```{r}
#| label: climate-correlations

# Beetle genetic variation and temperature
beetle_temp <- cor.test(
  beetles$Temperature,
  beetles$GenVarArapat,
  method = "pearson" )

# Beetle genetic variation and precipitation
beetle_precip <- cor.test(
  beetles$Precipitation,
  beetles$GenVarArapat,
  method = "pearson" )

# Plant genetic variation and temperature
plant_temp <- cor.test(
  beetles$Temperature,
  beetles$GenVarEuphli,
  method = "pearson" )

# Plant genetic variation and precipitation
plant_precip <- cor.test(
  beetles$Precipitation,
  beetles$GenVarEuphli,
  method = "pearson" )

# Print all four test results
beetle_temp
beetle_precip
plant_temp
plant_precip
```

## Results 

The correlation results summarize the direction and strength of the relationships between climate and genetic variation in each species (@tbl-climate-correlations). The significant negative association between temperature and beetle genetic variation is shown in @fig-beetle-temperature.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-climate-correlations
#| tbl-cap: "Pearson correlations between climate and genetic variation in the beetle and plant. P-values are unadjusted for multiple testing."

correlation_results <- tibble(
  Species = c("Beetle", "Beetle", "Plant", "Plant"),
  Climate = c(
    "Temperature", "Precipitation",
    "Temperature", "Precipitation" ),
  r = c(
    unname(beetle_temp$estimate),
    unname(beetle_precip$estimate),
    unname(plant_temp$estimate),
    unname(plant_precip$estimate) ),
  t = c(
    unname(beetle_temp$statistic),
    unname(beetle_precip$statistic),
    unname(plant_temp$statistic),
    unname(plant_precip$statistic) ),
  df = c(
    unname(beetle_temp$parameter),
    unname(beetle_precip$parameter),
    unname(plant_temp$parameter),
    unname(plant_precip$parameter) ),
  p = c(
    beetle_temp$p.value,
    beetle_precip$p.value,
    plant_temp$p.value,
    plant_precip$p.value ) )

knitr::kable(
  correlation_results,
  digits = c(0, 0, 3, 3, 0, 4),
  col.names = c(
    "Species", "Climate variable", "Pearson's r",
    "t", "df", "p-value" ) )
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-beetle-temperature
#| fig-cap: "Beetle genetic variation in relation to annual mean temperature at the sampling sites. The line shows a fitted linear regression, and the shaded band represents its 95% confidence interval for the mean response."
#| fig-width: 7

#| message: false

ggplot(
  data = st_drop_geometry(beetles),
  aes(x = Temperature, y = GenVarArapat) ) +

```

```{r}
#| label: reporting-values

N <- nrow(beetles)

temp_min <- format(min(beetles$Temperature), digits = 3)
temp_max <- format(max(beetles$Temperature), digits = 3)

precip_min <- format(min(beetles$Precipitation), digits = 3)
precip_max <- format(max(beetles$Precipitation), digits = 3)

bt_r <- format(unname(beetle_temp$estimate), digits = 3)
bt_t <- format(unname(beetle_temp$statistic), digits = 3)
bt_p <- format(beetle_temp$p.value, digits = 3)

bp_r <- format(unname(beetle_precip$estimate), digits = 3)
bp_p <- format(beetle_precip$p.value, digits = 3)

pt_r <- format(unname(plant_temp$estimate), digits = 3)
pt_p <- format(plant_temp$p.value, digits = 3)

pp_r <- format(unname(plant_precip$estimate), digits = 3)
pp_p <- format(plant_precip$p.value, digits = 3)
```

The `r N` sampling sites ranged from `r temp_min` to `r temp_max` °C in annual mean temperature and from `r precip_min` to `r precip_max` mm in annual precipitation. The climate maps show the regional patterns and sampling locations (@fig-temperature; @fig-precipitation). Beetle genetic variation was negatively associated with temperature (Pearson's *r* = `r bt_r`, *t* = `r bt_t`, *p* = `r bt_p`), with lower genetic variation generally occurring at warmer sites (@fig-beetle-temperature). Its relationship with precipitation was also negative but was not statistically significant (*r* = `r bp_r`, *p* = `r bp_p`). Plant genetic variation was not significantly associated with temperature (*r* = `r pt_r`, *p* = `r pt_p`) or precipitation (*r* = `r pp_r`, *p* = `r pp_p`). Of the four tests, only the beetle–temperature relationship was significant at the unadjusted 0.05 level (@tbl-climate-correlations).

## Interpretation

The clearest pattern was that beetle genetic variation tended to be lower at warmer sites. Plant genetic variation did not show a significant relationship with either temperature or precipitation, and precipitation was not significantly associated with beetle genetic variation. The species therefore did not show the same observed pattern, although these separate tests do not establish that their responses to climate are statistically different. Temperature may be relevant to the beetle’s genetic variation, but this correlation does not show that warmer conditions directly cause lower variation. Other factors, such as population size, isolation, and movement between populations, could also contribute to the pattern. Because the tests were not adjusted for multiple comparisons, the significant result should be interpreted cautiously.

## Questions

::: {.callout-tip title="Question 1: Color palettes"}

Which kind of palette (sequential, diverging, or qualitative) did you use for each map, and why does it fit that variable?

:::

Both maps use sequential palettes because temperature and precipitation are continuous variables that progress from lower to higher values. The temperature map moves from light yellow to dark red as temperatures increase, while the precipitation map moves from light blue to dark blue as precipitation increases.

::: {.callout-tip title="Question 2: Interpreting raster cells"}

Each climate value you extracted comes from a single cell about 1 km on a side. What does that one number actually represent for the beetles or plants at that site, and when could that be misleading?

:::

Each extracted value represents an estimate of long-term annual mean temperature or annual precipitation for the raster cell containing the sampling site, rather than a direct measurement of conditions experienced by individual beetles or plants. This can be misleading when local conditions vary within the cell, such as shaded versus exposed areas or differences in elevation, or when seasonal extremes are hidden by the annual summary.

## References

Fick, S.E. and R.J. Hijmans. 2017. WorldClim 2: new 1km spatial resolution climate surfaces for global land areas. *International Journal of Climatology* 37(12): 4302–4315.
